quote: The rainbow was explained. The haunts in the air, and gnomes in the mine, were explained away.
content: The essay gives no criterion for which is which, and the case it chose is the one where the criterion is least clear. A rainbow is a virtual image: it has no location in the world, moves as the observer moves, is seen differently by each eye, and cannot be approached or touched; on the account of levels in the previous essay it is a pattern in a multi-level map, and on the Mind Projection account of the essay before that it is at least as observer-dependent as sexiness. The socks test (does the causal chain behind the belief run through the thing believed in?) returns: the belief in the rainbow runs through raindrops, sunlight and the geometry of the observer’s eye, not through any object called a rainbow, just as the belief in the mirage runs through skylight and a temperature gradient. Whether one says the rainbow was “explained” and the mirage “explained away” is a decision about which of the folk description’s commitments one chooses to keep, which is what the eliminativism debate has been about since Churchland (1981). The essay’s method delivers the folk verdict the reader already held, and the reader keeps the rainbow because the reader likes rainbows. Keats would have had a point about that.

quote: If reductionism is correct, then even your belief in reductionism is just the mere result of the motion of molecules—why should I listen to anything you say?
content: The essay answers the weakest form of the argument and leaves the stronger form standing, and the stronger form uses premises this book supplies. The version the essay refutes says a caused belief is a discredited belief, and the socks example is a fair reply: caused by the fact is fine. The version that has a literature (Plantinga’s evolutionary argument against naturalism, 1993; Street (2006) for the evaluative case) says that the specific cause, natural selection, tracks fitness rather than truth for beliefs remote from survival, so that the causal chain behind such beliefs resembles the mirage more than the socks. Book I and the essays on evolution insist on exactly that premise (“evolution is a hack,” the biases, the leaky generalizations), and the belief in reductionism, in Bayes as law, and in mathematics as the substance of reality are beliefs about which no causal chain runs through the truth-makers, as the annotation on Righting a Wrong Question notes. The essay’s answer works where perception is concerned and does not reach the beliefs the objector was actually asking about; the “mere” it removes was never the point.
